newsitem.title: UK: Blair's arms plan gets guarded Adams welcome.
newsitem.headline: Blair's arms plan gets guarded Adams welcome.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair unveiled bold proposals on Wednesday for disarming rival Northern Irish guerrillas.

Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA's political arm, welcomed the plan, which was agreed in advance with the Irish government in Dublin. But he warned that wrangling over guerrilla disarmament could still hamper moves for a Northern Ireland settlement.
Blair said he hoped for a political settlement by next May in one of the world's longest-running and most intractable guerrilla conflicts.
The initiative envisages an independent commission to oversee the "decommissioning" of arms in parallel with progress on substantive aspects of a political settlement.

Blair told parliament that if the proposals were acceptable to all the parties, political talks that have marked time since they were launched a year ago should start in earnest by early September and conclude by next May at the latest.
"That is an ambitious target, but I have no doubt it is achievable if all concerned put their minds fully to it...

"There is no time to waste. The situation on the ground in Northern Ireland is fragile," Blair said, alluding to fears that this summer's annual round of street parades would trigger renewed sectarian violence in the province.
In a further symbol of the tension in Northern Ireland, police in south Belfast foiled a guerrilla ambush just hours before Blair spoke, security forces said.

The proposal for "parallel decommissioning", originally made in January 1996 by George Mitchell, the former U.S. senator chairing the Belfast peace talks, is aimed at luring Sinn Fein, the political wing of the anti-British Irish Republican Army, into the negotiations.

The term means the outlawed IRA, which wants a united Ireland, and rival Protestant guerrillas who want Northern Ireland to remain part of Britain, would give up their arms in stages while talks proceeded.

Blair's predecessor, John Major, rejected this element of Mitchell's proposals and demanded that arms be given up before the guerrillas -- who would prefer not to disarm ahead of a final settlement -- could enter talks.
Adams, the president of Sinn Fein, urged Blair to spell out how he aims to ensure that crucial all-party peace talks would not be disrupted if the arms row resurfaced.

"We will give the proposals published today by the two governments our fullest attention and consideration, and we welcome the proposal by the two governments to remove (arms) decommissioning as an obstacle to the commencement of substantive negotiations," Adams said in a statement. issued in Belfast.
"Having said that, I remain deeply concerned that the decommissioning issue will become a block to the negotiation of the substantive issues further down the road.

"We are informed that the two governments have committed themselves to ensuring that this will not happen... If this is the case there needs to be a clear understanding of how the British government intends to do this," he added.
Blair reiterated that the IRA would have to restore unequivocally the ceasefire it ended in February 1996 before Sinn Fein would be admitted to the talks.
"The settlement train is leaving, with or without Sinn Fein. If they want to join, it is absolutely clear what they have to do.
"I have dealt straight with them. I expect straight dealing in return. We and the other parties will not be waiting around for them," Blair said.

He confirmed his government had written to Sinn Fein on June 13 saying it could join the talks six weeks after a ceasefire -- only to have the offer brutally rejected three days later when the IRA murdered two policemen in the town of Lurgan.
"The credibility gap the IRA and Sinn Fein have to bridge is wider than ever after Lurgan," Blair said.
In a separate development, police in Northern Ireland said they had charged a 29-year-old man with the Lurgan murders and he would appear in court later in the day.

David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionists, the main party representing Northern Ireland's pro-British Protestant majority, said Blair's proposals were "seriously deficient" but he was careful not to reject them.
More than 3,200 civilians, police, soldiers and guerrillas have been killed in Northern Ireland's sectarian conflict since 1969.
